title: A Faithful Man in Nineveh
sum: Tobit introduces himself. He is from Naphtali, one of the northern tribes, carried off to Nineveh by the Assyrians. When his whole tribe worshiped Jeroboam's calf, he alone went to Jerusalem with his tithes and offerings. In exile he refused Gentile food, gave bread and clothing to the poor, and buried the bodies of Israelites the kings had thrown outside the city wall.

His goodness costs him. Under Sennacherib, an informer reports his burials; Tobit flees and loses everything except his wife Anna and his son Tobias. Then Sennacherib is murdered, and Tobit's nephew Ahiqar, now Esarhaddon's chief minister, speaks for him, and he comes home. The chapter sets out the book's themes: faithfulness far from the temple, alms, burial, family, and a God who works quietly through events.
readings: Read as a model life

Tobit's memoir lists the duties of a faithful Jew in exile: worship at the one temple while it can be reached, keep the food laws, give alms, bury the dead, marry within the people. Catholic and Orthodox readers have long read him as a saint whose example teaches the works of mercy.
Read as a story set in the past

The chapter's history is loose: it skips Sargon II, makes Sennacherib Shalmaneser's son, and joins events decades apart. Most scholars read it as a tale written long after, using famous names (Sennacherib, Ahiqar) the way a historical novel does, to teach how to live faithfully under foreign rulers.

views.C: Catholic readers find in Tobit a model of the corporal works of mercy, above all burying the dead, which the Church lists among them (Catechism 2447). The Church's teaching on inspired books allows that a sacred writer may use the form of a story to teach truth (Dei Verbum 12), so the loose chronology does not trouble its reading.
views.O: Orthodox readers honor Tobit and Tobias as righteous men of the Old Testament, and read the chapter as an icon of faithful life in a hostile world: worship, fasting from defiled food, and mercy to the poor and the dead.
views.P: Protestants have generally read Tobit as edifying but not authoritative. The chapter's historical errors were cited by Reformation-era writers as one reason it should not be used to establish doctrine; its picture of faithfulness in exile is still widely admired.
views.H: Scholars date the book to about 225–175 BC. The memoir form and the court setting borrow from the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar, which the author knew; Ahiqar becomes Tobit's nephew. The historical slips suggest an author far from the events, writing a story, not a chronicle. Fragments of Tobit in Aramaic and Hebrew from Qumran (4Q196–200) support the longer text followed here (Fitzmyer).
views.J: Tobit's piety looks forward to later Judaism: three tithes, avoiding Gentile bread, burial of the dead as a chief good deed (in the Talmud gemilut chasadim, deeds of loving-kindness, include burying the dead). Medieval Jewish retellings of Tobit in Hebrew and Aramaic kept the story alive even though it was not in the Jewish Bible.

echoes: 2 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 17:6; 1 Kings 12:28–30; Deuteronomy 12:5; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Deuteronomy 16:16; Daniel 1:8; 2 Kings 19:35–37; Isaiah 58:7; Matthew 25:35–36; Nehemiah 1:11

settings.what: Tobit's own account of his life
settings.to: the reader, as a memoir of an old man looking back on his life in exile
settings.when: after his return to Nineveh under Esarhaddon, in the story's world (about 680 BC)
settings.why: To present himself as a faithful Israelite who kept the law when his tribe did not, gave alms and buried the dead, and suffered for it, so that what follows reads as the test of a righteous man.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. The memoir showed them how to stay faithful when the temple was far away, when Gentile rulers were capricious, and when doing right could cost everything; and it gave them hope that God's providence works even through court politics.
views: The memoir is meant to be admired without reserve, as the Vulgate reads it (2:12–14 Vulgate).
Many recent scholars hear some irony: Tobit's self-praise sets up a fall that teaches him dependence on God (see 2:13–14).
Some scholars place the author among the eastern exiles in Mesopotamia, where the story is set, and point to its Persian names and its use of the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar.
Others point to the mistaken geography of Media (5:6), the book's concern for Jerusalem and the Qumran copies, and place it in Judea or Egypt. There is no agreement.

title: Feast Turned to Mourning
sum: At Pentecost Tobit's dinner is ready, and he sends Tobias to find a poor man to share it. Tobias comes back with news of a murdered Jew lying in the marketplace. Tobit leaves his food untouched, hides the body until dark, eats in grief remembering Amos's words, and buries the man at night while his neighbors laugh at him.

That night, sleeping in the courtyard, he is blinded by sparrow droppings; doctors make it worse. For years his nephew Ahiqar supports him, then his wife Anna works for wages. When her employers give her a young goat, Tobit accuses her of stealing it, and she answers with the sharpest line in the book: "Where are your alms now?"
readings: Read as a test like Job's

A righteous man loses his health and his means in the very act of doing good, and his wife mocks his piety. The Vulgate makes the comparison explicit (2:12 Vulgate: an example of patience "as also of holy Job").
Read as a story of a flawed hero
Tobit's goodness is real, but so are his pride and suspicion. Anna is right about the goat. The chapter shows a good man brought low so that he can learn to rely on God's mercy, not his own record.

views.C: Catholic tradition reads Tobit's burial of the dead as one of the corporal works of mercy and his blindness as a trial permitted by God, following the Vulgate: "that an example might be given to posterity of his patience" (Vulgate 2:12, Douay translation).
views.O: Orthodox readers see Tobit's leaving the feast for the dead man as an icon of mercy that sets love above ritual joy, and his suffering as the trial of the righteous that ends in God's visitation.
views.P: Protestant readers have often admired the scene's moral seriousness while noting that Tobit's suffering is not explained by any sin and is not presented as merit. Anna's protest is read as a warning against trusting in one's own good deeds.
views.H: Scholars note the Greek-period details (the month Dystrus, Elymais) and the Job pattern. Most read the quarrel as deliberate characterization: the author lets the reader see Tobit's faults.
views.J: The scene reflects Jewish values later put into law: burying a met mitzvah, an abandoned corpse, overrides even other commandments, and touching the dead makes one unclean (Numbers 19). Tobit's washing and waiting for sunset fit that practice.

echoes: Amos 8:10; Deuteronomy 16:11; Deuteronomy 21:23; Numbers 19:11–13; Job 2:9; Exodus 22:1–4; Mark 5:26

settings.to: each other, at the Pentecost dinner
settings.when: at the Feast of Weeks, after Tobit's return
settings.why: Tobit's order keeps the law's command to rejoice at the feast with the poor (Deuteronomy 16:11); the report turns the feast into mourning.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. Far from the temple, they could still keep the feasts at home and share them with the poor.

settings.when: eating after he has hidden the body
settings.why: The old word against Bethel's festivals has come true in his own life; for a northern Israelite it also confirms that the exile is God's judgment.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. The prophets were already read as Scripture, and Tobit's use of Amos taught them to read their own history through it.

settings.when: the evening he buries the murdered man, after his return from hiding
settings.why: To mock a man who risks his life again for the very deed that nearly cost him everything; the jeer shows how strange his piety looks from outside.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. Faithful Jews among Gentiles, and among careless fellow Jews, knew what it was to be laughed at for keeping God's law.

settings.to: Tobit, who has accused her of theft
settings.when: years into his blindness, when she supports the household
settings.why: To answer an unjust charge by turning his own virtues against him; her words drive him to the prayer of chapter 3.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. The scene let them see that piety can sour into self-righteousness, and that suffering tests a marriage.

traditions.q: Tobit risks his life to bury the dead (1:17–19; 2:3–8). Is burying the dead a sacred duty, and may Christians choose cremation?
views: Burying the dead is a corporal work of mercy that honors the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (Catechism 2300; 2447). Cremation is allowed unless chosen for reasons contrary to Christian teaching (canon 1176 §3), but the ashes must be kept in a sacred place, not scattered or kept at home.
Burial in the earth, as Christ was buried, is the Church's only practice. Cremation by choice is not accepted, and the Church of Greece and others refuse the funeral service to those who choose it.

The Prayer Book commits the body to the ground, "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection." Most Anglican churches today also permit cremation with the same service.

The dead should be decently buried, but without ceremony: the Westminster Directory calls kneeling and praying by or toward the dead body superstitious, and lays aside praying, reading and singing at the grave because they have been "grossly abused". It requires only that the body be decently buried. Cremation is a matter of Christian freedom for most Reformed churches today.

title: Two Prayers on One Day
sum: Stung by Anna's words, Tobit prays. He declares God just, confesses his own sins and his people's, accepts the exile as deserved, and asks to die. On the same day, far away in Ecbatana, a young woman named Sarah is taunted by her father's maid: seven husbands have died on their wedding nights, killed by the demon Asmodeus. Sarah climbs to an upper room to hang herself, then stops for her father's sake and prays instead.

Both prayers are heard at the same moment "before the glory of God." God sends the angel Raphael, whose name means "God heals," to heal both: to clear Tobit's eyes and to give Sarah to Tobias as his wife, setting her free from the demon. The reader now knows how the story will end; the characters do not.
readings: Read as a lesson in prayer
Two people in despair bring it honestly to God, even asking for death, and God answers both with more than they asked. The chapter models confession (Tobit) and trust (Sarah).
Read as the turn of the plot
The narrator steps in to tell the reader that heaven has already acted. The rest of the book is the slow working out, through ordinary choices, of what God decided here.

views.C: Catholic readers see in the two answered prayers the communion of heaven and earth: God hears the humble, and sends an angel as his minister. Raphael is honored as an archangel (feast with Michael and Gabriel, 29 September). Both prayers are read at Mass in the weekday lectionary (Tobit 3:1–11a, 16–17a, Wednesday of the Ninth Week, Year I).
views.O: Orthodox readers honor Raphael among the archangels at the Synaxis of Michael and the other Bodiless Powers (8 November) and read the chapter as showing that God hears the prayers of the afflicted and sends his holy angels to serve them (Hebrews 1:14).
views.P: Protestants value the prayers as fine examples of Jewish piety. They note that the 66 books name no angel Raphael, and they place their confidence in God's hearing prayer through Christ, not in angels' mediation.
views.H: The chapter interlaces two plots, a technique of Greek-era storytelling. Asmodeus probably has a Persian name. The two prayers follow the forms of Jewish prayer of the Second Temple period (praise, confession, petition).
views.J: Tobit's prayer has the pattern of the penitential prayers of Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9, and Sarah's opens with the blessing formula of later Jewish prayer. Asmodeus reappears in the Talmud as Ashmedai, king of demons.

echoes: Psalm 25:10; Daniel 9:4–19; Deuteronomy 28:37; Numbers 11:15; 1 Kings 19:4; Genesis 42:38; Daniel 6:10; Numbers 36:6–9

settings.when: the day Anna rebukes him, years into his blindness
settings.why: To confess that God is just and that he and his people deserve the exile, and to ask for death as release from grief and insult.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. They knew the exile was still not ended; the prayer gave them words to accept God's judgment, confess their sins and still ask for mercy. It also showed them that a righteous man may honestly ask to die.

settings.when: after Sarah has rebuked or struck her
settings.why: To wound her by blaming her for her husbands' deaths and wishing her childless.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. In a society where a woman's worth was tied to marriage and children, the taunt names the deepest shame.

settings.when: in her father's upper room, about to hang herself
settings.why: She weighs her father's shame and grief and decides to pray rather than kill herself.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. The scene showed that despair can be brought to God, and that love for others can hold a person back from death.

settings.to: God, with hands spread toward the window
settings.when: the same hour as Tobit's prayer
settings.why: To bless God, declare her innocence, explain why she has no kinsman to marry, and ask God either to take her life or to hear her shame.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. It gave a young woman's voice to the prayers of the faithful; Jewish women in the diaspora, often powerless, heard that God listens to them as much as to the righteous elder.

title: A Father's Charge
sum: Expecting to die, Tobit remembers the ten talents he left with Gabael in Rages and calls Tobias to give him his last instructions. He asks to be buried well, tells his son to honor his mother and to bury her beside him, and to keep the Lord in mind and do what is right.

Then comes a little book of wisdom: give alms from what you have, much or little, for alms rescue from death; avoid sexual sin and marry within your father's family, as the patriarchs did; pay workers the same day; do not do to others what you hate; do not get drunk; share bread and clothing; seek advice; bless God always. Only at the end does he mention the money: do not be afraid that we are poor, for the fear of God is wealth enough.
readings: Read as wisdom for everyone

The instructions sum up the ethics of Proverbs and the law for a family in exile. Jews and Christians have quoted them for two thousand years, especially the negative Golden Rule (4:15) and the praise of almsgiving (4:7–11).
Read as the book's program
Everything Tobias will do in chapters 5–14 follows this speech: he seeks a kinsman's daughter, pays his guide, prays, and buries his parents. The plot shows the instructions bearing fruit.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads 4:7–11 with 12:8–9 as Scripture's teaching that almsgiving, with prayer and fasting, expresses conversion and helps to make up for sin, never apart from grace (Catechism 1434; 1969; 2447). The Vulgate's "alms deliver from all sin and from death" (Vulgate 4:11, Douay translation) was long cited in this sense.
views.O: Orthodox teachers, following John Chrysostom, read the chapter as a call to mercy, the greatest of virtues after love of God, by which the faithful become like the merciful God and receive mercy.
views.P: Protestant churches value the moral teaching and many printed it in their Bibles between the Testaments. But they deny that alms take away sin or merit salvation: forgiveness comes by faith in Christ alone, and good works are its fruit (Westminster Confession 16.5).
views.H: Scholars read 4:3–21 as a wisdom instruction like Proverbs 1–9 and Sirach, close in places to the sayings of Ahiqar. The verses missing in Sinaiticus (4:7–19a) are known from Vaticanus and the Old Latin (Fitzmyer).
views.J: Tobit's instruction is a landmark of Jewish ethics: the negative form of the Golden Rule, later famous from Hillel; the conviction that tsedaqah, charity, saves from death (Proverbs 10:2), which Jewish custom still calls out at funerals and the High Holy Day liturgy echoes ("repentance, prayer and charity turn aside the evil decree"); and marriage within the people as faithfulness.

deep.b: Codex Sinaiticus, the main witness to the longer text, breaks off after "and to all who do what is right" in 4:6 and resumes in the middle of 4:19 with "the Lord will give them good counsel." The physical cause is not known, but the join is telling: the text runs straight from the words that end 4:6 into the middle of a sentence of 4:19, which is the mark of a copyist who skipped a stretch of the copy in front of him. For 4:7–19a the Plain therefore translates Vaticanus, the shorter Greek text, and each verse has a variant entry saying so. This matters for some of Tobit's best-known lines: "alms rescue from death" (4:10), the advice to marry within the tribe (4:12), the Golden Rule (4:15) and "bread on the grave of the righteous" (4:17) are all read from Vaticanus. Scholars also use the Old Latin translation, which follows the longer text, to reconstruct what Sinaiticus lost.

echoes: Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:4; Daniel 4:27; Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 12:33; Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:15; Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 7:12; Genesis 24:3–4; Numbers 36:8; Exodus 20:12; 1 Samuel 2:6–7

settings.when: the day he has prayed for death
settings.why: Having asked to die, he turns to practical duty: his son must know about the money left in Media.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. The thought of death leads a father to set his house in order, as faithful families were expected to do.

settings.to: his son Tobias, a young man about to take charge of the family
settings.when: the day of his prayer for death, before telling him of the money in Media
settings.why: To hand on the whole of a faithful life before he dies: care for parents, fear of God, generosity, sexual purity and marriage within the family, fairness to workers, sobriety, prayer. In the story it prepares Tobias for the journey and the marriage to come.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. It was a short handbook for keeping a Jewish family faithful in a Gentile world, where intermarriage, poverty and the loss of the temple threatened the community's survival. Its stress on alms and kin marriage answers those dangers.
views: Most read it as the book's teaching for every reader.
Some see a father's sincere but narrow counsel, which the story both honors and widens (Raphael, not Tobit, makes the marriage happen).

traditions.q: "Alms rescue from death" (4:10; compare 12:9, "Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin"). Does giving to the poor take away sin?
views: Yes, within grace. Almsgiving, with prayer and fasting, expresses conversion and obtains pardon for sins (Catechism 1434). Christ's forgiveness takes away the guilt of sin, but the sinner must still make satisfaction, "make amends" for the harm sin leaves, and works of mercy are among the penances the Church gives (Catechism 1459–1460). Cyprian built a treatise on Tobit's words. (On faith, works and merit, see the card at Joshua 2.)

Almsgiving heals the soul and draws God's mercy; John Chrysostom calls it a cure for sins and urges it with prayer and fasting. It is not a payment but a share in God's own mercy, part of the life of repentance and growth in God.

No. The Roman Confutation of 1530 cited Tobit 4:10 against the Lutherans; Melanchthon's Apology replied that forgiveness is received by faith for Christ's sake, and that Tobit speaks of alms that follow faith (Apology IV.156–158). Such alms please God, and Melanchthon grants that they "merit" many benefits from God and lessen punishments, but not forgiveness itself (IV.157).

The Book of Homilies quotes Tobit with approval, but explains that alms "wash away our sins" only because God, by grace, accounts the merciful as clean; nothing may obscure "the price of Christ's blood, who only wrought our purgation." Good works are the fruit of faith, not its cause.
No. Our best works cannot merit pardon of sin; they are accepted only in Christ. Tobit is not Scripture and cannot establish such a doctrine (Westminster Confession 1.3; 16.5).
Works of mercy are a means of grace, necessary for growing in holiness, and Wesley urged them strongly; but justification is by faith alone, and works cannot atone for sin.

traditions.q: Tobit tells his son to marry within his father's family (4:12), and Tobias marries a kinswoman. How closely related may a Christian couple be?
views: Marriage is invalid between blood relatives up to the fourth degree of the side line, which includes first cousins. The bishop can dispense for cousins, and even for uncle and niece, but never for parent and child or brother and sister (Code of Canon Law, canons 1078 and 1091).
Orthodox canon law forbids marriage between first cousins, as the Council in Trullo ruled (canon 54); later Orthodox practice extended the ban to more distant relatives as well.
Only the degrees forbidden in Leviticus 18 bind Christians; Luther attacked the medieval extension of the ban and held that cousins may marry.
Marriage must not be within the degrees forbidden in the Word (Leviticus 18); the Westminster Confession adds no ban on cousins.

title: The Stranger Who Knew the Way
sum: Tobias agrees to go to Media but asks how: he does not know Gabael or the road. Tobit gives him his half of the receipt and tells him to find a trustworthy guide. Outside, Tobias finds Raphael, who does not reveal that he is an angel. The stranger says he knows Media well and has stayed with Gabael.

Tobit questions the young man about his family; he calls himself Azariah son of Hananiah, a kinsman of good stock. Wages are agreed, and Tobit sends the two off with a blessing: may God's angel go with you. Anna weeps for her son and wishes the money had never mattered. Tobit comforts her: a good angel will go with him, and he will come home safe.
readings: Read as comedy and irony
The reader knows the guide is an angel; Tobit interviews him about his tribe and haggles over a drachma a day, and prays for an angel to go with them. The chapter is gentle, warm and funny.
Read as a picture of providence
God's help arrives looking like an ordinary hired man. The book teaches readers to trust that God is at work in everyday meetings, even when no one sees him.

views.C: Catholic tradition reads Raphael's care for Tobias as a picture of the guardian angel given to each believer (Catechism 336), and the Church honors Raphael as patron of travelers and of the sick.
views.O: Orthodox Christians pray daily to their guardian angels and read this chapter as a picture of that ministry: an unseen companion sent by God to guide and protect.
views.P: Protestants affirm that God sends angels to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), but are cautious about personal guardian angels and do not pray to angels. They value the chapter's picture of quiet providence.
views.H: Some scholars compare the folktale of "the grateful dead," in which a man who buried a stranger is helped by the dead man's spirit to win a bride whose earlier husbands died. They also note the dramatic irony and anachronisms such as the drachma. The geography of Media is mistaken.
views.J: The angel who goes before the traveler recalls Genesis 24 and Exodus 23:20. Later Jewish prayer for travelers (tefillat ha-derekh) asks God to guard the way, and the Talmud tells of two ministering angels who accompany a person home from the synagogue on the eve of the Sabbath (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119b).

echoes: Genesis 24:7; Genesis 24:40; Exodus 23:20; Psalm 91:11; Psalm 34:7; Hebrews 13:2; Matthew 18:10; Judges 13:16; Jeremiah 32:10–14

settings.why: He promises obedience and then raises the practical problems: he does not know Gabael, has no proof of who he is, and does not know the road.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. A dutiful son's honest questions were a model of obedience that still thinks; the problems he names set up God's answer in the guide.

settings.why: To show how Tobias can prove his claim and to send him with a trustworthy guide.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. Diaspora Jews traded and traveled across empires and kept money with kin in distant cities; the details were familiar.

settings.what: The guide's words and the hiring
settings.why: Raphael wins their trust with knowledge of the road and of Tobit's own family, and promises healing; Tobit makes sure the guide is a faithful Israelite.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. They would enjoy the irony, and learn that God's help may come in a form no one expects.
views: The angel's name and family are a fitting disguise, true in meaning ("the LORD helps").
The story lets the angel deceive for a good end; the book is not concerned with the question.

settings.why: Tobit entrusts his son to God and his angel; Anna voices a mother's fear and the cost of the money; Tobit answers with faith in the good angel.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. Many families in the diaspora sent sons on long journeys; the blessing gave them words of trust.

traditions.q: Tobit says "a good angel will go with him" (5:22), and Raphael guards Tobias all the way. Does each believer have a guardian angel?
views: Yes. "From its beginning until death human life is surrounded by their watchful care and intercession. Beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd" (Catechism 336, quoting Basil). The Church keeps a feast of the Guardian Angels on 2 October.
Yes. Each Christian receives a guardian angel, and the daily morning and evening prayers include a prayer to one's guardian angel.
Angels guard God's people, and Luther's morning and evening prayers ask, "Let your holy angel be with me, so that the evil foe may have no power over me." Lutherans do not pray to angels.
God appoints angels to care for each of us, but whether each believer has one particular angel is uncertain; Calvin would not affirm it, and warned against curiosity about it (Institutes 1.14.7).

Many evangelicals believe angels protect believers (Psalm 91:11; Hebrews 1:14) and some, like Billy Graham, speak freely of their help, but most hold that Scripture does not teach one angel for each person and reject praying to angels.

title: The Fish and the Bride
sum: On the first night, by the Tigris, a large fish leaps at Tobias's foot. The angel tells him to catch it and keep its gall, heart and liver: smoke from the heart and liver drives off demons, and the gall heals white films on the eyes. As they near Ecbatana, Raphael tells Tobias they will stay with his relative Raguel, whose only daughter Sarah he has the first right to marry.

Tobias is afraid: he has heard of the seven husbands and the demon, and he is his parents' only son. Raphael reminds him of his father's command to marry within the family, tells him to burn the fish's heart and liver in the bridal room and to pray with Sarah before they come together, and assures him that she was meant for him from before the ages. Tobias falls in love with her before he has met her.
readings: Read as a folktale
Monster fish, magic remedies, a bride whose husbands die on the wedding night, a demon lover: the chapter uses folktale motifs known from many cultures, retold to show God's care.
Read as a marriage teaching

The danger is overcome by obedience, prayer and trust, and the marriage is set within God's plan. Christian readers, especially through the Vulgate, have long used the chapter to teach the holiness of marriage.

views.C: Catholic readers take the fish as a God-given means of healing and deliverance, the power being God's through his angel. The Vulgate's longer speech (6:16–22), with its three nights of prayer and its warning against marrying for lust alone, shaped Catholic reading of marriage for centuries.
views.O: Orthodox readers see in Raphael's instructions the Church's own pattern: demons are driven off by prayer and by God's gifts, and marriage begins with prayer and blessing. The Orthodox marriage service, too, begins and ends in prayer and asks God to bless the couple as he blessed the patriarchs and their wives. (The wedding reading from Tobit 8 belongs to the Catholic and Anglican lectionaries, not the Orthodox service.)
views.P: Protestant readers have often found the fish remedy one of the clearest signs that Tobit is not Scripture: it looks like magic, unlike the Bible's exorcisms by word and prayer. Others note that Tobias and Sarah's prayer, not the smoke, is what the story stresses.
views.H: Scholars compare the 'monster in the bridal chamber' motif in world folklore and note Mesopotamian fumigation rites and ancient fish-gall eye remedies. The chapter's legal claims (6:13) do not match the law of Moses.
views.J: Asmodeus became Ashmedai, king of demons, in the Talmud. The idea that marriages are made in heaven (6:18) appears in the rabbis (Sotah 2a), and the prayer before the wedding night anticipates the Jewish wedding blessings.

echoes: Mark 1:25; Matthew 8:16; Mark 8:23; John 9:6; Numbers 36:6–9; Ruth 3:12–13; Genesis 2:24; Genesis 24:14; Proverbs 31:10

settings.when: the first night of the journey
settings.why: To give Tobias, without yet telling him why, the means of freeing Sarah and healing his father.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. Many feared demons and sickness; the story told them that God provides remedies and protection, and that the power belongs to him.

settings.what: Raphael's counsel about Sarah, and Tobias's fear
settings.why: To persuade a frightened young man to claim his kinswoman, remind him of his father's command, and give him the way to defeat the demon: smoke and prayer.
settings.readers: Jews of the last centuries BC, in the diaspora (Mesopotamia, Egypt) and in Judea itself, where copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were read at Qumran; where the book was written is debated. For Jewish families worried about marrying their children within the community, the scene presented kin marriage as God's plan and a marriage begun in prayer as safe from evil.

traditions.q: Raphael teaches Tobias to drive off a demon with smoke and prayer (6:8; 6:17–18). Do demons still trouble people, and how should the church drive them out?
views: Yes. The Church performs simple exorcisms at baptism, and a solemn exorcism may be done only by a priest with the bishop's permission, after medical causes are ruled out, using the approved rite in Christ's name (Catechism 1673; canon 1172).

Yes. The Church prays prayers of exorcism over every catechumen before baptism, renouncing Satan and his works, and the service books also contain exorcism prayers that priests read over those afflicted by evil spirits.
Luther kept a short exorcism in his baptism order (1523, 1526); many Lutheran churches later dropped it. Against the devil, Lutherans rely on the Word, prayer and the sacraments.
Demons are real, but there is no rite of exorcism; Calvin rejected exorcism as an added ceremony of baptism (Institutes 4.15.19). The church resists the devil with the Word and prayer.

Yes. Believers may cast out demons in Jesus' name (Mark 16:17), and deliverance ministry is part of the life of many Pentecostal and charismatic churches. They are divided on whether a born-again Christian can be troubled by a demon: deliverance teachers such as Derek Prince hold that believers can be "demonized" and need deliverance, while others in the movement deny it.
